beats.narration_text: Bula — this is Liam, in for Bear. There is a Brutalist skill called godot-gamedev. Most fellows read that name and assume it writes Godot game code for you. It does not. So I asked Claude to read the full skill and explain what actually happens when you point it at a game.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — hesitant writer BLUF. Misconception corrected: 'game-maker' → 'game-reader'. lead_silence_s required for typing head-start. seed 4065 = deterministic for this slug.
beats.narration_text: The name fools you. godot-gamedev is a game reader, not a maker. It takes a Godot project you already built and produces a teaching film that explains how it works — component by component, traced from actual source.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW — concept illustration, not a UI beat. Shows the skill's input→phase→output flow. FRAMEWORK beat satisfying teaching-arc checklist.
beats.narration_text: Here is the flow. You supply a path to a Godot project — the folder that contains the project-dot-godot file. Claude reads every runtime script, groups related components, and traces ownership and dependencies. It writes a beat sheet, generates narration, and the pipeline renders a four-K teaching film.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW — GodotDevWorkbench teaching illustration (code mode). Shows what the skill produces when reading a player script. WORKED EXAMPLE satisfying teaching-arc checklist. Labeled as teaching illustration per SKILL.md requirement.
beats.narration_text: When the skill runs on a real game, Claude starts with project-dot-godot: config, autoloads, input map, renderer settings. Then it reads every runtime script. The teaching unit is a pair: one focused, readable excerpt — then immediately the visible result that excerpt produces in the game. A verbal description alone is not a result.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW — SkillTeardownMechanism. Design tell: 'Label reconstructed editor views — Godot editor reconstruction' (VERBATIM QUOTE LAW). The disclosure requirement that makes this skill honest.
beats.narration_text: The design tell is explicit in the skill file: label reconstructed editor views as Godot editor reconstruction, and supply source path and line numbers. The skill cannot draw a plausible-looking scene tree and call it the game. Every node, property, and texture path must come from a file Claude actually read. Code-result pairs are logged in the evidence ledger as teaching-contract-v1.

props.heading: Reconstruct — don't invent.
props.body: Every displayed node, property, and texture path must come from a file Claude actually read. Plausible-looking output is not evidence. Code-result pairs are logged in evidence as `teaching_contract: 'code-then-result-v1'`.
props.quote: Label reconstructed editor views 'Godot editor reconstruction' and provide source path/line numbers. They are teaching views, not recordings of a live editing session. Never invent a debugger success line or a property value.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW — GodotDevWorkbench tree mode. Shows the scene-tree reading: saved scene vs runtime instance distinction. Different mode from B04, separated by B05 per ILLUSTRATE LAW.
beats.narration_text: Beyond scripts, the skill reads saved scene files. Every dot-tscn reveals which nodes exist in a saved scene — but not which nodes exist at runtime. Code-created nodes do not appear in a saved file. The skill requires this distinction: saved scene versus runtime instance. A diagram that conflates the two is not evidence — it is invention.

beats.narration_text: godot-gamedev is one of two Godot skills in this toolkit. The other is godot-walkthrough. The distinction is the question asked. Walkthrough asks: how does the player experience the game — level by level. gamedev asks: how does the code make that experience — component by component. Same project, two films, different lens.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW — SkillTeardownMechanism. SELF-DEMO limitation documented honestly per skill-teardown modifier feasibility fallback. Not faked, not skipped — named plainly.
beats.narration_text: The self-demo gate is honest about its limit. To actually run godot-gamedev, you need a real Godot game with a project-dot-godot file. The skill runs a coverage check first — art godot-gamedev dash-dash-check. This reel shows the mechanism and the output scenes; a full end-to-end build requires bringing a game project as input.

props.heading: Self-demo needs a real game.
props.body: godot-gamedev requires a game project with project.godot as input. This reel shows the mechanism and output scenes; a full end-to-end build needs a real game.
props.quote: Run `./art godot-gamedev --check REEL --game GODOT_PROJECT` before rendering and at handoff. It checks file coverage, hashes, source lines and beat references, not explanatory truth or visual quality.
props.sparkLine: Bring a game. Get a film.

beats.role_note: ClaudeVerdictArtifact — verdict beat. Recapitulates implemented work, limitations, and honest judgment. NO source required on verdict beats (teaching arc: no-source-no-verdict exempts recapitulation).
beats.narration_text: What the skill gets right: it mandates code-and-result pairs — each excerpt is immediately followed by the game consequence, not deferred to a summary. It makes the evidence contract explicit: reconstruct, don't invent. The limitation is clear: this is a reader, not an omniscient explainer. Give it a shallow game and the teaching film will be shallow too.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk with greeting 'Your turn.' Liam reads the prompt aloud and discusses it. Signs off 'Liam, in for Bear.' per IN-FOR-BEAR LAW.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the paste-ready prompt. 'Read skills-slash-make-slash-godot-gamedev-slash-SKILL-dot-M-D in full. I have a Godot 4 project at [path]. Produce a complete beat sheet for a godot-gamedev teaching film, standard mode. For each major component, name where it lives in the project, what data enters it, what it changes, and what the player sees.' Replace [path] with any Godot 4 project folder you have. When Claude comes back, check the component inventory against what you know about the game. If it misses a system, ask it to read that specific file and trace the dependency. The check is the work. Liam, in for Bear.
